extracted.intended_audience: clinical researchers, trialists, journal editors, and readers interested in reporting quality of randomized controlled trials
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and classifying 'spin' in reports of parallel-group randomized controlled trials whose clearly identified primary outcome is statistically nonsignificant, and methods for measuring its frequency. Useful for those assessing or preparing trial reports to avoid misleading presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "spin"
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific reporting strategies, whatever their motive, to highlight that the experimental treatment is beneficial, despite a statistically nonsignificant difference for the primary outcome, or to distract the reader from statistically nonsignificant results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a descriptive definition used to identify biased or misleading presentations; motive is irrelevant to the classification. Use this definition as the core criterion when determining whether reporting distorts trial findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary outcome clearly identified and statistically nonsignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Include only parallel-group RCTs with a clearly identified primary outcome showing statistically nonsignificant results (ie, P > or = .05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A necessary precondition for assessing "spin" in this study: the trial must state a primary outcome and that outcome must not achieve statistical significance by the stated threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in the title
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial title is reported with spin (eg, implying benefit despite nonsignificant primary outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should not overstate effectiveness when primary outcomes are nonsignificant; screening titles is part of detecting misleading presentation. The paper reports the proportion of articles with spun titles as an indicator of reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in abstract — Results section
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin identified in the Results section of the abstract (eg, selective emphasis of favorable secondary findings or subgroup analyses while primary outcome nonsignificant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract Results should accurately reflect the primary outcome; emphasizing other analyses to imply benefit constitutes spin. The study reports frequency of this occurrence to quantify misreporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in abstract — Conclusions section
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin identified in the Conclusions section of the abstract, including conclusions that focus only on treatment effectiveness despite a nonsignificant primary outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract Conclusions must not assert effectiveness when the primary outcome is nonsignificant; focusing solely on treatment effectiveness in conclusions is a common form of spin and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in main-text — Results section
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin identified in the main-text Results section (eg, presenting secondary or subgroup findings in ways that imply overall benefit despite nonsignificant primary outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main Results should prioritize the primary outcome and not be framed to obscure nonsignificance. The study quantifies how often Result sections contain such spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in main-text — Discussion section
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin identified in the main-text Discussion (eg, interpreting nonsignificant findings as evidence of benefit, overstating clinical relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions should interpret results in light of nonsignificant primary outcomes; overstating benefits or downplaying nonsignificance is classified as spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin in main-text — Conclusions section
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin identified in the main-text Conclusions (eg, concluding effectiveness despite nonsignificant primary outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions must reflect the actual results of the primary outcome; concluding benefit when the primary outcome is nonsignificant is a clear instance of spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin present across multiple sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of spin in at least two of the evaluated main-text sections (Results, Discussion, Conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cumulative presence of spin across sections as a marker of pervasive misreporting; the study reports that more than 40% had spin in ≥2 main-text sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data abstraction and reviewer process for detecting spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Two readers appraised each selected article using a pretested, standardized data abstraction form developed in a pilot test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent dual review and a piloted standardized form to reliably identify instances of spin; this procedural standard reduces subjective error in classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report prevalence estimates with confidence intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting frequencies of spin (eg, percent articles with spin in a given section), provide 95% confidence intervals alongside percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting point estimates with 95% CIs communicates precision and uncertainty of prevalence measures (the abstract reports percentages with 95% CIs for each measured item).
